articles.full_text:
झारखंड में अगले तीन दिन बढ़ेगा तापमान, 9-10 सितंबर को बारिश के आसार
प्रतीकात्मक फोटो
झारखंड में अगले तीन दिनों तक तापमान में 2-3 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बढ़ोतरी होगी, जिससे उमस बढ़ेगी. 8 सितंबर को बंगाल की खाड़ी में निम्न दबाव बनने की संभावना है, जिसके असर से 9-10 सितंबर को राज्य में वज्रपात के साथ बारिश हो सकती है.
Jharkhand Weather Update: झारखंड में फिलहाल तेज बारिश की उम्मीद कम है. मौसम विभाग का कहना है कि अगले तीन दिनों में राज्य का अधिकतम तापमान 2-3 डिग्री सेल्सियस बढ़ सकता है. तापमान बढ़ने के साथ मौसम में उमस भी बढ़ेगी. जिससे लोगों को थोड़ी गर्मी और उमस का सामना करना पड़ सकता है.
आपके शहर में
बंगाल की खाड़ी में बन रहा निम्न दबाव
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 8 सितंबर को बंगाल की खाड़ी में निम्न दबाव का क्षेत्र बनने की संभावना है. इसके प्रभाव से 9 और 10 सितंबर को रांची समेत झारखंड के कई जिलों में मौसम का मिजाज बदल सकता है. इस दौरान वज्रपात और तेज हवा के साथ बारिश होने की संभावना है.
शुक्रवार को रांची में छिटपुट बारिश
शुक्रवार को रांची में छिटपुट बारिश हुई, जबकि लातेहार में तीन मिमी बारिश दर्ज की गयी. राज्य के बाकी हिस्सों में बारिश नहीं हुई. हालांकि, मौसम में बदलाव के बीच सभी जिलों के अधिकतम तापमान में बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की गयी. बारिश की यह स्थानीय स्थिति कुल तापमान को प्रभावित कर रही है.
2.4 डिग्री बढ़ा शहर का तापमान
रांची का अधिकतम तापमान शुक्रवार को 27.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. यह पिछले दिन की तुलना में 2.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस ज़्यादा रहा. मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, अगले कुछ दिनों में तापमान में और बढ़ोतरी हो सकती है, लेकिन 9-10 सितंबर को बारिश की गतिविधियां बढ़ने के आसार हैं.

Southeast Asia’s extreme heat exposes holes in safety net for outdoor workers
Many Southeast Asian cities lack adequate heat risk assessments, and have weak regulations protecting outdoor workers, a report says
Oil palms younger than three years offer little shade, so he tends them in the early mornings and evenings, spraying pesticide, applying fertiliser or weeding. “We try our best to avoid going to the plantation around noon,” Chung said.
He carries extra drinking water and, as a smallholder, decides when to slow down or change his hours.
But not everyone shares that luxury. Many construction, agriculture and platform workers across Southeast Asia lack that flexibility because employers or output determine their schedules.
Southeast Asia is getting hotter, with the annual mean temperature rising by 0.14 degrees Celsius (0.25 degrees Fahrenheit) to 0.2 degrees per decade since the 1960s, according to an Asian Development Bank report in June.
Many Southeast Asian cities lacked adequate heat risk assessments, and regulations protecting outdoor workers from extreme heat were either weak or unenforced, the report said.

The August heat was a killer for retail footfall and it also seemed to suppress spending on discretionary categories, the latest BDO High Street Sales Tracker showed on Friday (4 September).
The UK’s total sales across all discretionary categories grew just 2.2% in August, below August’s average across the last eight years, excluding the Covid-19 period.
High street footfall fell as record summer temperatures kept shoppers away from stores and August marked the sixth month this year to record below inflation growth, meaning sales volumes have declined as retailers prepare to head into the Golden Quarter.
Total sales across the discretionary retail categories had grown by 3.9% in the same month last year as August is traditionally a strong month for retail sales as back-to-school shopping and new autumn ranges help drive demand.
But this year failed to deliver. Store sales grew 3.6%, compared to 5.2% last August, while non-store sales increased 2.3%, significantly below the 6.6% recorded last year.
Fashion specifically was weak. Fashion like-for-like sales increased by 1% versus 4.4% in August 2025. And while store-based fashion sales were up 5.4%, non-store sales were flat. This compares to +5.8% for store and +8.2% for non-store sales in August 2025 and suggests it wasn’t only heat causing a problem. Many consumers were clearly just not in the mood for shopping.
Sophie Michael, head of Retail and Wholesale at BDO, said: “The record-breaking heat may have made headlines this summer, but it hasn’t led to a boost in consumer spending.
“However, the weather can’t be the only thing to blame for yet another lacklustre month. Whilst August is traditionally a strong month for the sector, this disappointing set of figures points to deeper issues where consumers remain reluctant to spend on non-essential items.
“Despite consumer confidence reaching a two-year high following the appointment of a new Prime Minister and reflecting the so-called ‘Burnham Bounce’, this may be short-lived as energy bills are set to rise again in October and households face continued cost pressures.
“As we prepare to enter the so-called Golden Quarter, the most crucial time of year for the sector, retailers may have already made decisions about order volumes ahead of Christmas.
“After a disappointing Golden Quarter last year, with continued geopolitical uncertainty and the potential impact on costs and supply chains, many will understandably be nervous about getting those decisions wrong.
“With the first Budget under the new Prime Minister and Chancellor due at the end of October, pressure is likely to grow on the Government to provide targeted support for retailers as they brace for the most important trading period of the year.”

articles.title: Morocco’s 2026 heatwaves in numbers: Is extreme heat becoming the new normal? - HESPRESS English - Morocco News

articles.full_text:
Morocco spent much of the summer of 2026 under repeated bouts of extreme heat, with temperatures repeatedly exceeding 40°C and approaching 50°C in some parts of the country.
By July 26, Morocco had already experienced four heatwaves in three months, according to the national meteorological service.
During one episode in late July, temperatures reached 44°C to 47°C in parts of the south and southeast, while some areas recorded temperatures as much as 12°C above seasonal averages.
How hot did it get?
On July 1, more than nine Moroccan cities recorded temperatures above 40°C. Kenitra reached 42.2°C, while Salé recorded 40°C. Even Casablanca, whose Atlantic location normally moderates summer temperatures, reached 33.4°C.
The heat intensified by mid-July. On July 17, 12 cities recorded temperatures above 40°C, with Taourirt reaching 46°C, Oujda 45.7°C and Zagora 43.5°C. Tetouan, which generally experiences milder temperatures than inland areas, reached 40.3°C.
Another heatwave began around July 20, bringing temperatures of 44°C to 47°C to parts of southern and southeastern Morocco.
The following week, the national meteorological service warned that temperatures could again reach 46°C in inland and southern areas.
A further heatwave was forecast from July 29 to Aug. 1, with temperatures expected to reach 47°C in several provinces.
Is 2026 breaking heat records?
Morocco’s national temperature record remains 50.4°C, recorded in Agadir on Aug. 11, 2023. It was the first time temperatures in the country exceeded 50°C.
July 2024 also brought extreme temperatures, including 47.7°C in Beni Mellal and 47.6°C in Marrakech.
The national meteorological service described July 2024 as having two successive heatwaves, including one that lasted 10 days.
But the significance of Morocco’s recent heat is not limited to whether a particular year breaks the national temperature record.
There are growing indications that the country’s baseline temperatures are becoming warmer, with average temperatures increasingly exceeding what was considered normal in previous decades.
Another indicator is the frequency of unusually warm days, as temperatures increasingly rise well above seasonal averages across different parts of the country. Areas that typically experience milder conditions are also occasionally exposed to extreme heat.
High temperatures are also arriving earlier in the year rather than being confined to the peak of summer. This can extend the period during which people, crops and water resources are exposed to heat stress.
During recent heatwaves, Morocco has repeatedly recorded temperatures several degrees above seasonal norms, with some episodes producing departures of more than 10°C.
Those departures can be as important as individual temperature records because they show how unusual the conditions are for a particular location and time of year.
The repeated occurrence of such episodes raises a broader question for Morocco: whether extreme heat is becoming an increasingly persistent feature of the country’s climate rather than an occasional summer anomaly.

articles.title: Extreme heat can affect major organs, even for people accustomed to Mid-South summers - FOX13 Memphis
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands

After months of high temperatures, people living in the Mid-South may feel like their bodies have gotten used to the heat.
To a certain extent, doctors say they have. But becoming accustomed to hot weather does not make someone immune to heat-related illness.
Extreme heat forces the body to work harder to maintain a safe internal temperature. As the body heats up, blood flow increases toward the skin to help release heat and sweating helps cool the body.
But sweating also causes the body to lose water and electrolytes. With prolonged exposure, the strain can begin to affect multiple organs.
Dr. Dale Criner, chief medical officer at Methodist Germantown Hospital, said repeated exposure without adequate hydration can take a toll.
“Obviously if you’re out there working in the temperatures all summer long without hydrating yourself, it can take a cumulative effect,” Dr. Criner said.
In severe cases, heat stroke can begin damaging cells and organs throughout the body.
The brain, heart, kidneys, liver, and muscles can all be affected. The heart also has to work harder to maintain circulation as the body attempts to cool itself, while dehydration can put additional stress on the kidneys.
Severe heat illness can also cause muscle tissue to break down, which doctors say can be life threatening.
“Unfortunately, every year we see people who do succumb to heat related illnesses that do have heat strokes, and we have had some patients that have passed away in the Mid-South,” Dr. Criner said.
There is some truth to the idea that someone who regularly experiences Mid-South summers may become better at handling hot weather.
The process is known as heat acclimatization. With repeated exposure, the body can make adjustments that help it cope with heat more efficiently, such as changes in sweating and circulation.
Dr. Avianne Robinson, a family medicine resident physician at Baptist Memorial Hospital said people may notice the difference when they move between climates.
“You kind of get used to a certain climate, but it’s still the same thing,” Dr. Robinson said. “If you’re overdoing it, you’re not staying well hydrated. You’re just as susceptible to heat related illness.”
Dr. Criner said the amount of time someone spends in extreme conditions matters, regardless of how accustomed they are to hot weather.
“Heat is heat,” Dr. Criner said. “And whether you’re out in it for 15 minutes in June, you get used to it in July, you can still be affected the same way. It’s the amount of time that you’re out in the elements that really makes a difference.”
There can also be another problem after months of hot weather: People may become less vigilant about taking precautions.
Webb Smith, a clinical exercise physiologist at Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital and an associate professor in the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center, said people can develop a type of fatigue around constantly preparing for the heat.
Smith said even people accustomed to hot weather should continue taking precautions, including staying hydrated, limiting prolonged exposure and taking breaks to cool down.

High temperatures: what to expect this weekend in France
Seven departments have been placed on orange heatwave alert for this weekend
Heatwave alerts have been extended in southern France with temperatures expected to reach 40C in some parts of the country this weekend.
For this weekend, Météo-France has placed seven departments under orange heatwave alert: Ardèche, Aude, Drôme, Gard, Hérault, Pyrénées-Orientales and Vaucluse
A further 10 departments are under yellow heatwave alert on Saturday: Ariège, Bouches-du-Rhône, Haute-Garonne, Gers, Isère, Landes, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, Hautes-Pyrénées, Rhône and Var.
On Sunday, the yellow alert extends to 13 departments, with Aveyron, Tarn and Tarn-et-Garonne also affected.
The four-level weather warning system ranges from green, meaning no particular vigilance, to yellow (be alert), orange (be very vigilant) and red (absolute vigilance).
Temperatures up to 40C
The highest temperatures this weekend will be concentrated in Languedoc and the Rhône valley.
On Saturday, maximum temperatures of 36C to 38C are expected across much of the region, with 39C to 40C possible in inland Languedoc.
Perpignan could reach 38C and Marseille 36C, while temperatures will be lower on the Riviera, with around 29C expected in Nice.
Further west, temperatures will remain high but will be slightly lower than on Friday. Toulouse could reach 35C, Bordeaux 34C and Limoges 33C.
Northern France will be much cooler, with highs of around 23C in Lille, 25C in Brest and 26C in Paris.
Heat to spread north on Sunday
The heat will continue on Sunday. Maximum temperatures are expected to reach 27C to 33C across northern France, with around 25C possible near the Channel.
In the south, temperatures will remain between 32C and 37C, with local highs of 36C to 38C in parts of Midi-Pyrénées and the lower Rhône valley.
The west of France could see more unsettled weather. Showers and isolated thunderstorms are possible from parts of Poitou-Charentes and Limousin towards the Pays de la Loire, Centre-Val de Loire, Normandy and Brittany.
The current heat comes after Météo-France confirmed that summer 2026 was the hottest summer recorded in France since measurements began in 1900.
The average temperature for June, July and August reached 24C, almost 1C above the previous record set in 2003.

Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for heavy rain in 15 districts on Saturday. These include Panchkula, Ambala, Yamunanagar, Kurukshetra, Kaithal, Karnal, Panipat, Sonipat, Mahendragarh, Rewari, Jhajjar, Gurugram, Faridabad, Nuh and Palwal. Strong winds are also likely in these districts.

The weather department said conditions would remain changeable in Sirsa, Fatehabad, Hisar, Bhiwani, Charkhi Dadri, Jind and Rohtak, with drizzle or rain possible at some places. Clouds were seen over Sonipat, Hisar and Panipat since morning.
According to the IMD, the monsoon trough is extending from Sriganganagar through Rohtak and Fatehgarh to the Bay of Bengal, and its effect could bring rain with winds across many parts of the state between September 5 and 7.
Rainfall and waterlogging
In the past 24 hours, Panchkula recorded the highest rainfall at 99 mm, followed by Yamunanagar at 57.5 mm, Gurugram at 44.5 mm, Karnal at 33.5 mm, Rohtak at 32 mm and Rewari at 20 mm. Waterlogging was reported in several areas. In Gurugram alone, 36 mm of rain fell within an hour on Friday, leading to waterlogging and traffic jams.

Monsoon may weaken after September 8
Weather scientist Dr Madan Khichar said rain with strong winds would continue in the northern and southern districts amid cloud cover, but monsoon activity may weaken again from September 8. He said day temperatures may fall slightly during the rain, while night temperatures may rise marginally. He advised farmers to postpone irrigation and pesticide spraying till the spell ends and ensure proper drainage in fields.
August rain below normal
Haryana received 135.4 mm of rain in August against the normal 146.1 mm, the lowest in three years. From June 1 to August 31, the state received 283.4 mm against the normal 349.9 mm, a deficit of about 19 per cent. The advisory came as several parts of Delhi-NCR witnessed intense rain, leading to widespread waterlogging near the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport, Anand Vihar, Connaught Place and other areas. The waterlogging also slowed traffic movement on several roads, affecting travel to the airport.

As many as 92 roads remain blocked across Himachal Pradesh following torrential rains, while 44 transformers and 25 drinking water supply schemes have been disrupted in the state.
As per the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC), Mandi has reported the highest number of blocked roads at 47, followed by Kullu with 22 and Kangra with eight. Sirmaur has five blocked roads, Una four, Solan three, Shimla two and Lahaul and Spiti one.
Of the 44 disrupted transformers, 23 are in Mandi, 11 in Kullu and 10 in Shimla, the SEOC said.
The rains have also affected drinking water supply schemes in several districts. Hamirpur has reported disruption to 17 schemes, while three each have been affected in in Solan and Chamba and two in Shimla.
Meanwhile, light to moderate rain is likely to continue in isolated places of the state.

Delhi crosses annual rainfall mark as IMD issues red alert for heavy rain
Delhi has crossed its annual rainfall average with nearly four months left in 2026, as the IMD issued a red alert for heavy rain and thunderstorms.
Delhi woke up to a second consecutive day of rain on Saturday, with the capital recording 804.7 mm of rainfall so far this year — already above its annual long-period average of 774.4 mm, with nearly four months still left in the year.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for most of the city amid forecasts of moderate to heavy rain and thunderstorms. Multiple spells of light to moderate rain are expected at many places, along with isolated heavy rain during the forenoon. Light to moderate rain is expected to continue at most places during the afternoon and evening.
From January 1 this year to 8:30 am on Saturday, the city recorded 804.7 mm of rain, as compared to the Indian Meteorological Department’s yearly long-period average of 774.4 mm. The city had crossed the mark by 5:30 pm on Friday itself, recording 32.6 mm of rain, bringing the city’s total rainfall to 800 mm.

The rainfall recorded at the IMD’s weather station in Safdarjung in a month is taken as the city’s total rainfall for that month, as the station is considered representative of the city’s weather.
Multiple parts of Delhi experienced light showers late on Friday night and early Saturday morning. The IMD stated that from Saturday morning to 10:30 am, Narayana recorded 12.5 mm of rain, followed by Safdarjung (10.6 mm), Pragati Maidan (9.6 mm), Lodhi Road (7.5 mm), and Mayur Vihar SPS (5 mm).
At around 10:20 am, the IMD issued a red alert for almost the entire city, barring the westernmost part of southwest Delhi. “Moderate to Heavy Rain moderate Thunderstorm with Lightning (wind speed 50-60 kmph) very likely over Delhi. of the western half of the ciry, and an orange alert for the eastern half,” it stated.
The IMD has so far only predicted the possibility of very light to light rain on Sunday, while no rain is expected from Monday onwards.
The IMD categorizes rainfall up to 15.5 mm as light, between 15.6 mm and 64.4 mm as moderate, between 64.5 mm and 115.5 mm as heavy, and between 115.6 mm and 204.4 mm as very heavy.
The city’s air has also remained clean due to the weather, with the Air Quality Index being recorded at 58 at 11:05 am, in the “satisfactory” category.
Due to the rain, today’s maximum temperature is expected to be between 29°C and 31°C, as compared to the IMD’s normal maximum temperature for September 3 to 7 of 34.1°C.

articles.title: Belgrade Under Orange Alert, Here's What Batut Recommends - srpske.rs
articles.search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Planning to spend this afternoon outdoors? If you are in Belgrade, Loznica, Vrsac or Negotin, it is better to push that plan to the evening.
The Institute of Public Health of Serbia, Batut, issued a health weather alert this morning for Saturday, September 5. The orange level, meaning weather conditions are very dangerous to health, applies to the city of Belgrade and to the Macva, South Banat and Bor districts. The Institute names Surcin, Loznica, Vrsac and Negotin as the hardest hit spots, where daytime temperatures reach a category the Institute rates as very dangerous, up to 36 degrees Celsius.
A yellow level, meaning potentially dangerous weather, is in effect across most of the rest of Serbia. Only five locations in the entire country carry no warning at all.
Precision matters here, since outlets are not using identical wording today. Batut, along with Informer and Mondo in the body of their reports, describe an orange level of warning. Blic uses the word “critical” in its headline. The Institute’s official statement mentions only the orange level, and that is the figure this article carries.
Why today carries extra risk
High temperatures are arriving alongside strong sun. Serbia’s Hydrometeorological Institute is forecasting ultraviolet radiation of 6 and 7, on a scale that runs to 11, across the entire country today. That combination, heat stress plus a high UV index, is why the Institute is singling out young children, pregnant women, older people and those with chronic illness for extra caution. Their risk of heatstroke is considerably higher than for a healthy adult.
Five tips for hot days, straight from Batut
- Wear light colored clothing made of lightweight, breathable summer fabric
- Drink water throughout the day. Batut’s guidance calls for “regular rehydration throughout the day, regardless of physical activity”
- Avoid stepping out of air conditioned spaces during the hottest part of the day unless you have to
- If you must go outside, carry a bottle of water and drink from it before you feel thirsty
- Save heavier household chores and physical work for early morning or late evening
What the forecast says for today and tomorrow
Serbia’s Hydrometeorological Institute expects Belgrade’s low today to fall between 17 and 21 degrees, with a high near 36 degrees, alongside a light to moderate south wind. The picture is similar across the rest of the country. “It will be mostly sunny and very hot across Serbia today, with a light to moderate south wind,” the Institute wrote in its forecast for September 5. In the evening and overnight, first in Vojvodina and later in other parts of the country, brief cloud cover and the odd short lived shower are possible, with the wind shifting to the northwest and picking up.
Better news arrives as soon as tomorrow. According to the Hydrometeorological Institute, highs drop to around 30 to 31 degrees on Sunday, September 6, with lows ranging between 15 and 21 degrees. That continues the trend already reported before the weekend, when the Institute forecast highs of up to 37 degrees with real cooling not expected until September 10.
When the orange alert lifts
Until then, the plan is simple. Go out early in the morning or only after seven in the evening, carry water, and make sure children and older family members are never left without fluids and shade during the day. An orange alert is not a reason to panic, but it is a reason to plan today a little differently than usual.
